title: The basics
lead: Short and useful: spirit or liqueur, amaro and vermouth, proof, the ordering words, and well, call and premium.

sections.name: Spirit or liqueur

lines.label: In short
lines.text: A liqueur is a spirit, sweetened.

know: Spirit is distilled: vodka, gin, rum, tequila, whiskey, brandy.
Liqueur is a spirit with sugar and flavor added.
15% is the EU minimum strength for a liqueur.
Orange liqueur, like triple sec or Cointreau, is in a Margarita.
sections.source: EU spirit drinks regulation 2019/787, Annex I (eur-lex.europa.eu)

sections.name: Amaro, vermouth and bitters
know: Amaro means “bitter”: herbal, bitter and sweet at once.
Aperitivo Aperol and Campari: lighter, for before dinner.
Vermouth is wine, flavored and fortified. Fridge once open.
Bitters go in a dash at a time, like Angostura.

sections.name: Proof and ABV
know: Abv is the share of alcohol in the bottle.
Proof in the US is twice the ABV.
80 Proof is 40% ABV.
Cask Strength is bottled near barrel strength, little water added.
sections.source: US TTB standards of identity, 27 CFR 5.143 (law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/27/5.143); EU spirit drinks regulation 2019/787, Annex I (eur-lex.europa.eu)

sections.name: Ordering words

lines.label: In short
lines.text: Neat, rocks, up, tall, a back.

know: Neat the spirit alone, no ice.
Rocks over ice.
Tall a taller glass with more mixer.
A Back something on the side, like a water back.

sections.name: Well, call and premium

lines.label: In short
lines.text: Ring in what the guest asked for.

know: Well is our house pour when no brand is named.
Call means the guest named the bottle.
Premium is the top shelf. It costs more.
Ring It In the way the guest ordered it.

read.bigIdea: A liqueur is a spirit, sweetened.
read.where: A **spirit** is distilled: vodka, gin, rum, tequila, whiskey and brandy are the base spirits. A **liqueur** is a spirit with **sugar and flavor** added. In the EU a liqueur is at least **15% ABV**, and most have at least **100 grams of sugar per liter**. Families you’ll hear: **orange** (triple sec, Cointreau), **coffee**, **nut**, **herbal** and **fruit and floral**.
read.mixup: **Sloe gin** and **Grand Marnier** sound like spirits, but they’re **liqueurs**.
read.sayIt: That’s a liqueur, so it’s sweeter and lower in alcohol than a spirit.

keyPoints.line: means “bitter”: herbal, bitter and sweet at once.
Aperol and Campari: lighter, for before dinner.
is wine, flavored and fortified. Fridge once open.
go in a dash at a time, like Angostura.

read.where: **Amaro** means “bitter” in Italian: herbal liqueurs that are bitter and sweet at once. **Aperol** and **Campari** are lighter, brighter bitters for before dinner. **Vermouth** is **wine** flavored with herbs and fortified: **sweet** for a Manhattan or Negroni, **dry** for a Martini. It’s wine, so once open it goes in the **fridge**. **Bitters**, like Angostura, are strong infusions added a **dash** at a time.
read.mixup: **Vermouth** isn’t a spirit. It’s wine, so it spoils like wine.
read.sayIt: Something after dinner? A Cognac, or an amaro?

keyPoints.line: is the share of alcohol in the bottle.
in the US is twice the ABV.
is 40% ABV.
is bottled near barrel strength, little water added.

read.where: **ABV** (alcohol by volume) is the share of alcohol in the bottle. In the US, **proof** is **twice** the ABV: a 40% whiskey is 80 proof. Vodka, gin and rum are at least **37.5%** in the EU; US whiskey is at least **40%**; a liqueur can be as low as **15%**. **Cask strength** means bottled close to the strength it came out of the barrel, with little or no water added.
read.sayIt: That one’s cask strength, so it’s stronger than most.

keyPoints.line: the spirit alone, no ice.
over ice.
a taller glass with more mixer.
something on the side, like a water back.

read.bigIdea: Neat, rocks, up, tall, a back.
read.where: **Neat** is the spirit alone, with no ice. **On the rocks** is over ice. **Up** means shaken or stirred with ice, then strained into a stemmed glass. **A splash** is a little of a mixer, like water or soda. **Tall** means a taller glass with more mixer. **A back** is something on the side, like a **water back**.
read.stopsTitle: Say it back to the guest
read.mixup: A **water back** is water on the side. **With water** means water in the drink.
read.sayIt: So that’s a bourbon on the rocks, with a water back.

keyPoints.line: is our house pour when no brand is named.
means the guest named the bottle.
is the top shelf. It costs more.
the way the guest ordered it.

read.bigIdea: Ring in what the guest asked for.
read.where: The **well** is the house pour: what goes in when a guest doesn’t name a brand. A **call** is when the guest names the bottle. **Premium** bottles are the **top shelf** and cost more. Ring in exactly what the guest ordered, so they get, and pay for, what they asked for. The **Back Bar** shows our bottles.
read.mixup: A guest who asks for “**your house vodka**” wants the **well**. A guest who names a brand wants that **call**.
read.sayIt: Any vodka you like, or our house vodka?

sources: EU spirit drinks regulation 2019/787, Annex I (eur-lex.europa.eu); Common bar practice; US TTB standards of identity, 27 CFR 5.143 (law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/27/5.143). Facts taken from the Level 2 lessons, which cite them. Written for Mise, Nov 12, 2026.

facts.fact: A spirit is distilled: vodka, gin, rum, tequila, whiskey and brandy are the base spirits. A liqueur is a spirit with sugar and flavor added. In the EU a liqueur is at least 15% ABV, and most have at least 100 grams of sugar per liter. Families you’ll hear: orange (triple sec, Cointreau), coffee, nut, herbal and fruit and floral.
facts.source: EU spirit drinks regulation 2019/787, Annex I (eur-lex.europa.eu)

facts.fact: Amaro means “bitter” in Italian: herbal liqueurs that are bitter and sweet at once. Aperol and Campari are lighter, brighter bitters for before dinner. Vermouth is wine flavored with herbs and fortified: sweet for a Manhattan or Negroni, dry for a Martini. It’s wine, so once open it goes in the fridge. Bitters, like Angostura, are strong infusions added a dash at a time.

ABV (alcohol by volume) is the share of alcohol in the bottle. In the US, proof is twice the ABV: a 40% whiskey is 80 proof. Vodka, gin and rum are at least 37.5% in the EU; US whiskey is at least 40%; a liqueur can be as low as 15%. Cask strength means bottled close to the strength it came out of the barrel, with little or no water added.
facts.source: US TTB standards of identity, 27 CFR 5.143 (law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/27/5.143); EU spirit drinks regulation 2019/787, Annex I (eur-lex.europa.eu)

facts.fact: Neat is the spirit alone, with no ice. On the rocks is over ice. Up means shaken or stirred with ice, then strained into a stemmed glass. A splash is a little of a mixer, like water or soda. Tall means a taller glass with more mixer. A back is something on the side, like a water back.

The well is the house pour: what goes in when a guest doesn’t name a brand. A call is when the guest names the bottle. Premium bottles are the top shelf and cost more. Ring in exactly what the guest ordered, so they get, and pay for, what they asked for. The Back Bar shows our bottles.

unverified: Amaro, vermouth and bitters descriptions are general bar knowledge; bar lead to confirm against our bottles.
Splash, tall and back are common US bar usage, not a rule; whether a tall pour costs more is the bar lead’s call.
